chapters.title: Chapter 3: Energy, Commodities, and Global Chokepoints

lessons.title: Why Crude Oil Still Moves Indian Markets: Understanding India's Import Dependence

body.text: India does not produce a war, a chokepoint closure, or an OPEC+ decision. It imports the large majority of the oil affected by all three, which is why a barrel of crude thousands of kilometres away still shows up in your fuel bill, your rupee, and your portfolio.

children.text: Chapters 1 and 2 mentioned crude oil repeatedly, in the four channels, in the Russia-Ukraine case study, and in India's discounted Russian oil trade. This chapter slows down and treats energy as the subject in its own right, starting with the single fact that makes India unusually sensitive to it: how much of its oil it has to buy from somewhere else.
The Number That Explains Almost Everything

stats.label: Crude import dependence
stats.context: The share of India's crude oil consumption met through imports, one of the highest among major economies

stats.label: Indian Basket
stats.context: The reference crude price India actually tracks, an average of Oman, Dubai, and Brent-linked sour and sweet grades, rather than Brent alone

stats.label: Rule of thumb
stats.context: Commonly cited estimate of the additional annual import bill for every sustained $10 per barrel rise in crude, though the exact figure moves with import volumes

children.text: Four Places a Crude Spike Shows Up

body.caption: How a Higher Oil Price Moves Through the Indian Economy

cells: Current account deficit and the rupee
A bigger import bill in dollars means more rupees sold to buy those dollars, widening the current account deficit and pressuring the rupee, reinforcing the currency channel from Chapter 1
Higher crude feeds into transport, logistics, and fuel costs across the economy, pushing up CPI and complicating the RBI's rate decisions
The government can cut fuel excise duty to cushion consumers during a spike, as it did in November 2021 and May 2022, but doing so directly reduces its own tax revenue
Crude-sensitive sectors, aviation, paints, tyres, and chemicals, see input costs rise directly, while refiners and oil producers are affected very differently, covered next

children.text: Upstream vs Downstream: Not Every Oil Stock Reacts the Same Way

A common mistake is treating 'oil stocks' as one uniform group. India's oil and gas companies split into two very different exposures, and a crude spike genuinely helps one side while squeezing the other.

body.title: Upstream Producers vs Downstream Refiners and Marketers

columns.label: Upstream (ONGC, Oil India)
points: Extracts crude oil and gas from the ground and sells it
Generally benefits when crude prices rise, since it earns more per barrel produced
Exposed to the opposite risk when crude prices fall sharply

columns.label: Downstream (IOC, BPCL, HPCL)
points: Buys crude, refines it into fuel, and sells it to consumers
Profitability depends more on the refining margin, the gap between crude cost and fuel selling price, than on the crude price level itself
A sharp, sudden crude spike can squeeze margins if retail prices cannot be raised as quickly as input costs rise

body.text: This is why 'crude oil is up' is not, by itself, enough information to decide whether it is good or bad news for a specific Indian energy stock. You need to know whether the company is upstream or downstream, and how quickly retail prices are likely to adjust.

children.text: How Petrol and Diesel Prices Actually Get Set in India

Petrol pricing was deregulated in June 2010 and diesel in November 2014, meaning oil marketing companies are formally free to revise retail prices daily, based on a rolling average of international crude prices and the rupee's exchange rate. In practice, prices have often shown periods of administered restraint, staying unchanged for stretches even as international crude moves, particularly around politically sensitive periods, before catching up later. A large portion of the retail price is also excise duty and state-level taxes, which is precisely the lever the central government adjusted in November 2021 and again in May 2022 to soften the impact of a crude spike on consumers.

body.title: One Crude Move, Two Different Stocks
body.scenario: Brent crude jumps 15 percent over two weeks following a Middle East escalation. You are evaluating two Indian holdings: an upstream oil producer, and a downstream refiner and fuel retailer.
body.prompt: Would you expect this crude spike to affect both companies the same way? Explain the likely difference.
body.modelAnswer: No. The upstream producer generally benefits from higher crude prices, since it earns more per barrel it sells. The downstream refiner and retailer's outcome depends on its refining margin and how quickly it can pass the higher crude cost through to retail prices, if retail prices are slow to adjust, a sharp crude spike can actually squeeze its margins in the near term, the opposite direction from the upstream producer.

body.title: The Indian Basket
body.question: India's 'Indian Basket' crude price, published by PPAC, is best described as:
options: The price of Brent crude alone
An average of Oman, Dubai, and Brent-linked crude grades that reflects what India actually imports
The retail petrol price at the pump
The price ONGC pays for domestic crude only
body.explanation: The Indian Basket blends sour crude, priced off Oman and Dubai benchmarks, and sweet crude, priced off Brent, to better reflect the actual mix of crude India imports, rather than tracking any single global benchmark alone.

body.title: Oil and the Indian Economy: Key Terms

cards.definition: The gap when a country's imports of goods, services, and transfers exceed its exports over a period, commonly widened by a rising oil import bill.
India's reference crude oil price, published by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), blending Oman, Dubai, and Brent-linked crude grades.
The difference between the value of refined petroleum products a refiner produces and the cost of the crude oil used to make them, the key profitability driver for downstream refiners.

Upstream refers to exploration and production of crude oil and gas. Downstream refers to refining crude into fuel and marketing it to consumers, a fundamentally different business with different price sensitivities.

points: India imports over 85 percent of the crude oil it consumes, which is the single structural fact behind why global oil shocks reach the Indian economy so directly

A crude spike shows up in four places at once: the current account deficit and rupee, retail inflation and RBI policy, government fiscal room through excise duty, and crude-sensitive corporate earnings

Upstream producers like ONGC and Oil India generally benefit from higher crude prices, while downstream refiners and marketers like IOC, BPCL, and HPCL depend more on refining margins and how quickly retail prices adjust, an important distinction before assuming 'oil stocks' all move together

Petrol and diesel pricing is formally deregulated and daily, but has often shown periods of administered restraint in practice, with excise duty as the government's main lever to cushion consumers during a spike
Understanding India's oil exposure sets up the next lesson: the physical chokepoints, like the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, where supply disruptions to this imported oil actually originate

body.text: Figures on import dependence, per-barrel fiscal impact, and specific policy dates are approximate and can change with updated government data or new policy decisions. This lesson references specific companies for educational, factual illustration only, and is not a recommendation regarding any company or sector.
